newsitem.title: USA: Tropical Storm Danny hovers off Louisiana coast.
newsitem.headline: Tropical Storm Danny hovers off Louisiana coast.

text.p: Tropical Storm Danny hovered ominously off the Lousiana coast on Thursday, where forecasters said it could gather strength and become a hurricane before moving ashore.

Its 60 mile-per-hour winds (96 kph) -- still for the most part out over the Gulf of Mexico -- whipped up high tides at Grand Isle, about 60 miles (96 km) south of New Orleans, forcing the evacuation of the area's 1500 residents.
"The main reason I ordered everybody out is because we got plenty (of) tourists on the island and I don't want nobody stuck here," Grand Isle Mayor Arthur Bellanger told Reuters.

Bellanger said 30 miles (50 km) of Louisiana Highway One, the only route out of Grand Isle, were expected to be under water on Friday when the slow-moving storm moved ashore. Coastal areas to the west in Terrebonne Parish were also being evacuated, he said.

Marshall Wickman, meteorologist for Houston-based private forecaster Wilkens Weather Technologies, told Reuters that Danny was likely to make landfall near Port Fourchon, La., just west of Grand Isle.

Forecasters predicted a storm surge of up to five feet (1.5 metres), with resulting flooding in low-lying areas of southern Louisiana. They said Danny could become a minimal hurricane, with winds of 74 miles per hour (119 kph) or above, as it fed off the warm waters of the Gulf of Mexico.

A hurricane watch was in effect from Cameron, La. to Orange Beach, Ala. The National Hurricane Centre in Miami said the storm was expected to drop rains of up to 10 inches (25 cm) in Louisiana and Mississippi.

On Thursday afternoon, Danny was located 110 miles (177 km) south southwest of New Orleans, or about 50 miles (80 km) off the coast. The storm was virtually stationary throughout the day and was expected to move northeast at the rate of just 2 miles per hour (3 kph), the hurricane centre said.
New Orleans officials closed flood gates and lowered the water level in area canals in preparation for the expected heavy rains. Most of the city is below sea level and susceptible to flooding.
In St. Bernard Parish, southeast of New Orleans, Emergency Preparedness Director Bob Brocamonte said sand bags were being placed along flood-prone roads.
Police said the storm had not yet caused many problems, but that several campers trapped by high water at a state park on Grand Isle had to be pulled to safety with tractors.

The U.S. Coast Guard received a distress call from two people on a 37-foot (11 metres) sailboat that developed engine problems about 35 miles (56 km) southeast of the storm and sent the cutter Paw Paw to assist.
"At the moment they are under way and under their own power, but they did call for our assistance," said Coast Guard Chief Buddy Dye.
Oil companies evacuated workers from offshore production platforms in the path of the storm.
"We're pulling about 100 non-operating personnel off various rigs and platforms," Texaco Inc. spokesman Pierre DeGruy said.
